tn.quote: Mon-Khmer languages, for the most part, are not tonal, but in Jeh phonemic high tone has been discovered. Sec. 4.2 'Vogais eco': the only word-final unstressed syllables are approximant + a vowel that copies the preceding stressed vowel ([ˈŋgoyo] 'água', [ˈŋĩɾĩ] 'criança', [ˈwowo] 'caído no chão'); presence and quality are predictable, so the echo vowel is excluded from the phonological representation (/ŋoy/, /ŋĩɾ/, /wow/; [ˈŋgo.yo] is phonologically one syllable) and the phonological word ends in its stressed syllable. tn.quote: Stress falls on the last syllable in both dialects … In contrast to Pazeh, pitch in Kaxabu is intrinsically related to stress, perhaps as a result of language contact. In Kaxabu, the stressed syllable has a high pitch (henceforth H). It follows a low pitch if the word is disyllabic, e.g., punu ‘head’ (L.H), or a mid pitch (M) if the word is trisyllabic, as in tulala ‘flower’ (L.M.H). … If a word contains a heavy syllable in initial position, the first syllable is H rather than L. In disyllabic words, the pitch is H.H, as in dauik ‘eye’.
